newsitem.title: USA: INSIGHT - U.S. T-bonds may not be out of woods yet.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT - U.S. T-bonds may not be out of woods yet.

text.p: U.S. Treasury bond futures are probably not out of the woods yet, despite a mild bounce in Friday morning trade after nearly a week of steady declines, technical analysts said.

The market was still correcting a rally from April lows that accelerated in late May and peaked last Friday, they said, adding that a strong rebound from here was unlikely, although the pullback had yet to damage the trend.
"It's reasonable...that we should see an attempt to stabilize here," said Terence Gabriel, technical analyst at I.D.E.A.

"However, given the fact that the directional momentum has now broken down and we as of yet have not fully corrected the overbought condition, the potential for a sustained gain off of this area is pretty limited," he noted.
September T-bond futures were up 12/32 on the day at 111-17/32 in late morning after dipping to a low of 111-2/32. They had hit a four-month high of 112-24/32 last Friday.

Gabriel saw various support/resistance levels coming in in the 111-00 to 111-9/32 zone and expected that area to have a gravitational effect against attempts to break out in either direction in the coming days.

In the longer term, he expected the market to test a trendline drawn from the January 1996 high and December 1996 high, now at around 113-1/2. But oscillators needed to fully refresh themselves to enable such a strong rise, he said.
David Ging, vice president at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette, agreed that the April-June advances called for a little deeper correction.
"We think we'll come back down a little past the tops of the old ranges, the highs we set back in May," he said, referring to the 110-1/4 area.

Ging said the market had run out of steam at 112-24/32, just short of a key Fibonacci retracement level at 112-28/32, and momentum indicators were now making bearish crossovers or, in some cases, bearish divergence.

Sentiment surveys were sending a sell signal and investors' cash reserves were at low levels, he said. He further noted that the commitment of traders report showed that large hedgers had been selling the longer end of the yield curve aggressively over the past two weeks.
"Take them all together and it says we've at least got to see a fairly decent correction," Ging said.
But he said good buying interest should re-emerge in the 110-1/4 area. He added that whether that support holds would be crucial in determining if the market's uptrend was still intact.
Analysts expected bonds to receive little inspiration from next week's Federal Open Market Committee meeting, at which most economists expect the Federal Reserve to hold interest rates steady.
"It's pretty well priced-in that the Fed's not going to do anything," Ging said.
